message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel, data‑intensive tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) with powerful, complex control logic, large caches, and sophisticated branch prediction. | Hundreds to thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput; each core is lightweight and shares resources. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC) with many features (branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution). | Very simple instruction set, often SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) – same operation applied to many data elements simultaneously. |
| **Execution Model** | Serial or lightly parallel – one thread runs on each core, but each core can execute multiple instructions per cycle. | Massive parallelism – thousands of threads run concurrently, each doing the same operation on different data. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory access, sophisticated prefetching. | Smaller per‑core caches, relies on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR) and large shared memory on the chip. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Control‑heavy tasks, branching code, small data sets, latency‑sensitive operations. | Data‑parallel tasks, matrix/vector operations, image/video processing, deep‑learning inference/training. |
| **Power Efficiency** | Optimized for low power per core, but overall power scales with number of cores. | Optimized for high throughput per watt – many cores share power budget. |
| **Programming Model** | Single‑threaded or multi‑threaded with OS scheduling; languages like C/C++, Java, Python. | Parallel programming frameworks (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute, Metal, DirectCompute); requires explicit parallelism. |

### Why the difference matters

* **Latency vs Throughput** – CPUs excel at low‑latency, single‑thread performance; GPUs excel at high throughput for many independent operations.
* **Branching** – CPUs handle divergent branches efficiently; GPUs suffer when threads in a warp diverge because they must serialize the divergent paths.
* **Precision & Flexibility** – CPUs support full 64‑bit integer and floating‑point precision, complex data types, and arbitrary memory access patterns. GPUs traditionally focused on 32‑bit floats and structured data, though modern GPUs now support mixed precision and more flexible memory models.

### Practical Takeaway

If you’re writing software that needs to perform many identical calculations on large data sets (e.g., matrix multiplication, convolution, particle simulation), a GPU can give you orders‑of‑magnitude speedup. If your code involves complex decision trees, system calls, or needs to run on devices without a dedicated GPU, a CPU is the right choice. In many modern systems, the CPU and GPU work together: the CPU orchestrates tasks and handles control flow, while the GPU crunches the heavy numerical work.
